STUDENT SOLDIERS EORT PRESIDENT WILSON TO
GREAT LABOR MEETING AT BUFFALO.

Student soldier of the Port Niagara training camp escorting President Wilson through Buffalo on his way to address the great meeting of the American Federation of Labor. The President made a stirring appeal to the workers assembled at the convention for their cooperation in the war for democracy. He declared Germany must be beaten before peace is possible and asked for the nation to present a united front to the enemy. The convention applauded the President's declarations and pledged its loyalty. 11/13/17.

There is no particular advantage in being a rioter no matter what your leanings are, when you know there is a special branch of the service, trained and ready to drive you to cover, if you become turbulent. This branch of the service will fall in line and if absolutely necessary will pump lead into the inciters of riots. In this photo the Second battalion of the Ninth Coast Defense Command, New York Guard, is demonstrating the formation which has proven to be effective in handling street rioters. The hollow square formation with machine gunners deployed in front of the square control the street while troopers with levelled rifles back them up. The soldiers on the side are covering the windows on both sides of the street. Military organizations all over the country will be specially drilled not because it is necessary, but just to be ready for eventualities.

For the first time in their history the United Con-deferate veterans are holding an annual re-union outside the bounds of the States which composed the Southern Confederacy. Their twenty-seventh annual re-union is now on at Washington, D.C. Thousands of the "vets" in the camp received a most cordial well-being on their arrival. It is a call for a renewed spirit of patriotism and warm co-operation with those into whose hands we have committed the welfare of our country."

The upper photograph shows C. P. Rogers, a Confed-erate veteran from Anderson, S.C., who is a point and who sells his poems for a nickel a copy.

An interesting Napoleonic relic has been discovered in the possession of Miss Sarah Forsyth, daughter of the late Jacob Forsyth of Chicago. It is the harness worn by horses which carried Napoleon Bonaparte to Silesia in 1812 in his retreat from Russia, when he left behind him the flaming ruins of Moscow. The harness, until it became the property of the late Mr. Forsyth, was owned by Bruno Ganzel, long since dead. It was left at the home of the grandfather of Ganzel, a public official in the Silesian village, where Napoleon stopped to change horses and to rest. The abandoned outfit was brought to this country by Bruno Ganzel, and was bought by Jacob Forsyth. The harness is made of fine leather and carried with it two groups of silverbells. It has the high bow effect characteristic of the Russian troika, to be worn by the middle horse, and is adorned xxx with silver ornaments.

The Altiscope rifle, that latest death-dealer to make its appearance.

The action of the rifle is similar to that of the submarine periscope, the firing being done after the aim is found through the reflecting lenses. The marksman is crouched far below the edge of the trench his entire lead being concealed from the enemy.

Taking the modern Springfield rifle, as used by the United States Army, the two inventors built into it a frame of compressed steel to lower or raise the barrel. They also added reflecting lenses to permit the marksman to hold the butt of the gun in the customary shoulder position and get his aim through the sights of the elevated barrel. In this way the barrel of the rifle projects over the edge of the trench while the marksman remains fully covered.

Experts who have examined the invention declare it to be as effective as the regular rifle and can be operated with a greater degree of safety by the soldier. It can be fired without raising the barrel or used as an altiscope gun at will.

The inventors are Mr. S. A. Guiberson, Jr. and Mr. L. L. Richards, both of Los Angeles, Calif. The rifle has had one exhibition before the War Department and the result of this trial while not bringing about the instand adoption of the gun was highly satisfactory. (FROM OUR SPECIAL CORRESPONDENT.)

LLANBERIS, Monday.—The War Office experiment of training officers in mountain warfare was commenced to-day at Llanberis, under the direction of Major Bruce, of the 5th Gurkhas, and Colonel Hoskins, of the Staff College.

The general idea of to-day's work was that Snowdonia was in the hands of a savage enemy, and that three columns of British troops, each 4,000 strong, had arrived overnight and were encamped in the Pass of Llanberis.

These imaginary columns would advance by separate routes to drive the enemy from the mountainous country around Llanberis, and to-day Major Bruce and the party took the line of route which the centre imaginary column would take.

Scouts are supposed to have climbed the nearer hills in the dead of night, and to have located the enemy, the column starting at dawn. The main body would extend in single file a length of ten miles, with mule transport and food for a week.
The whole campaign was gone through in imagination by the party. They are all young and, fresh from the hard training of the manoeuvres, appeared very fit.

Major Bruce set a hot pace, fortunately with intervals for short lectures, brief halts which were welcome to some at least; but the major found no need to pause for breath before plunging into his lecturete.
He is a noted mountaineer, and I am told by a sergeant who served under him that he is known in India as the King of the Gurkhas, and that he can do as much on the hills as the Gurkhas themselves.
His boots were made in India, and have rope soles studded with huge Pathan nails.
The twenty-eight officers were dressed in walking suits, and two or three wore shorts. One in particular who showed rather much knee was dubbed "the boy scout," to the general amusement.
From their headquarters at Pen-y-Gwryd the party will start each day and work out some fresh phase of mountain warfare for the fortnight over which the experiment extends.

This remarkable photograph was made during a $40,000 fire at an army post "Somewhere in the United States." The fire started at 11:30 on the evening of Oct. 24th, and before it could be brought under control many of the soldiers' quarters and much of their clothing had been consumed by the flames.

The soldier fire fighters can be seen at the right of the photograph forming a bucket brigade that is passing water to the men on the top of the building nearest the conflagration. The buckets pass down the line to the men on the ladder placed against the side of the building. They in turn lift the buckets up to the soldiers on the roof. One soldier is seen on the roof with bucket ready to dose the flames.

The roof of the building at the left has been ignited by the flying sparks and the soldiers not actively engaged in fighting the flames stand about watching the wonderful scenic effects of the conflagration. INSURED AND PASSED BY THE COMMITTEE OR PUBLIC INFORMATION. 10/51/17.
